tool.title: “Ready for the Homeland” in Croatian media: Commemorations, victory, and foundation
tool.excerpt: “Ready for the Homeland” in Croatian media: Commemorations, victory, and foundation. This article analyses the media discourse surrounding the WWII fascist salute Za dom spremni (ZDS) in the aftermath of two national commemorations that took place in Croatia in spring 2020: Jasenovac and Operation Flash (Bljesak). In spring 2020 Zoran Milanović, the newly elected President of Croatia, adamantly criticized the presence of the salute, associated with the collaborationist Ustaša regime, at the two commemorations, calling for its removal and ban. This led to heated reactions from war veterans and politicians who considered Milanović’s actions unacceptable and offensive towards the memory and legacy of the 1990s war, which triggered a wider debate regarding Croatia’s post-war national identity. The object of the analysis is the discourse surrounding the salute as it emerges in opinion pieces published in weekly and daily newspapers in April, May, and June 2020. With the salute becoming an increasingly prominent part of negotiating national identity and tailoring political agendas, investigating how it is justified, disapproved or otherwise challenged in the media is an aspect that deserves more attention. Relying on insights from discourse studies, the article sheds light on various statements that (de)legitimize the salute and consequently particular actors and actions associated with it. With the help of semiotics of culture wider signification tendencies and dominant discourse(s) upon which the national selfdescription has been built are identified. The article contributes to scholarship on hate speech and contested symbols in the post-Yugoslav space and their (mis)uses in societies struggling with traumatic legacies.

The president represents Croatia in international relations, serves as commander-in-chief of the armed forces, and performs key constitutional duties, including the appointment of the prime minister and the ratification of treaties.
History The office of the President of Croatia was established with the adoption of the Constitution of Croatia on December 22, 1990, during the final years of Yugoslavia.
Initially, the president was elected by the Parliament of Croatia , reflecting a parliamentary system with a ceremonial head of state.

Pre-Independence Era In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Croatia experienced a surge in nationalist sentiment and political mobilization, culminating in the 1990 parliamentary elections, the first multi-party elections since World War II.
These elections saw the victory of the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), led by Franjo Tuđman, who was subsequently elected president by parliament on May 30, 1990.

Post-Independence and Early Presidency (1990s) Following Croatia's declaration of independence on June 25, 1991, and the subsequent outbreak of the Croatian War of Independence , the presidency became a pivotal institution in the nation-building process.

The 1990 constitution was amended in 1991 to formalize Croatia's status as a sovereign state, and further amendments in 1998 introduced direct elections for the president, replacing the parliamentary selection process.
During this period, the president served as both head of state and de facto head of government, with the prime minister acting in a subordinate capacity.
A constitutional referendum held in November 2000 introduced sweeping changes that transformed Croatia's governance structure from a semi-presidential to a parliamentary republic.
The 2000 reforms marked a turning point in Croatian politics, diminishing the presidency's centrality in day-to-day governance and reinforcing the principle of parliamentary sovereignty.
Role and Powers The President of Croatia serves as the head of state, embodying the unity of the nation and representing Croatia both domestically and internationally.
Constitutional Duties The president's formal responsibilities include the appointment of the prime minister, who must command the confidence of the Parliament of Croatia .
The president also appoints judges to the Constitutional Court of Croatia , with the approval of parliament, ensuring judicial independence.
Representation and Diplomacy Internationally, the president represents Croatia in state visits, diplomatic negotiations, and international organizations.
Presidents often emphasize Croatia's role as a bridge between Central Europe and the Balkans, promoting regional cooperation and stability.
Election Process The President of Croatia is elected through a direct popular vote, reflecting the democratic principle of universal suffrage.

The electoral process is governed by the Constitution and the Law on the Election of the President of the Republic of Croatia, which outlines eligibility criteria, campaign regulations, and voting procedures.
Eligibility and Campaigning To be eligible for the presidency, a candidate must be a Croatian citizen aged at least 40, have resided in Croatia for at least 10 years, and not hold dual citizenship.
The most recent election, held in December 2024, saw the re-election of Zoran Milanović, who won 58% of the vote in the second round against Dragan Primorac, a former minister.
Turnout in presidential elections has fluctuated, with the 2020 election recording a 47% participation rate amid the COVID-19 pandemic.
Franjo Tuđman (1990–1999) Franjo Tuđman, founder of the Croatian Democratic Union , was Croatia's first president, elected by parliament in 1990 and subsequently re-elected in 1992 and 1997.

Ivo Josipović (2010–2015) Ivo Josipović, a law professor and member of the Social Democratic Party of Croatia , became president in 2010 as Croatia navigated the aftermath of the global financial crisis and the final stages of EU accession.
His presidency has focused on social welfare, judicial reform, and maintaining Croatia's pro-European stance.
As president, he has navigated tensions with the ruling Croatian Democratic Union government, reflecting the office's role as a check on executive power.
Notable Presidents and Their Legacies The legacy of Croatia's presidents is closely tied to the country's historical trajectory.
Stjepan Mesić is celebrated for his role in democratization, while Ivo Josipović's presidency symbolized Croatia's European aspirations.

Significance in Croatian Governance The presidency has played a crucial role in Croatia's political development, from its early days as a contested institution to its current status as a stabilizing force.

Today, the president serves as a guardian of the constitution, a diplomatic representative, and a symbol of national unity, contributing to Croatia's identity as a sovereign and integrated European state.

As Croatia continues to navigate its role within the European Union and the global community, the presidency remains a cornerstone of its constitutional framework, balancing ceremonial duties with strategic influence in shaping national policy and international relations.

tool.title: Hadronic processes at work in 5BZB J0630-2406
tool.excerpt: Hadronic processes at work in 5BZB J0630-2406. Recent observations are shedding light on the important role that active galactic nuclei (AGN) play in the production of high-energy neutrinos. In this study, we focus on one object, 5BZB J0630-2406, which is among the blazars recently proposed as associated with neutrino emission during the first 7-yr IceCube observations. Modelling the quasi-simultaneous, broad-band spectral energy distribution, we explore various scenarios from purely leptonic to lepto-hadronic models, testing the inclusion of external photon fields. This theoretical study provides a complementary testing ground for the proposed neutrino-blazar association. Despite being historically classified as a BL Lac, our study shows that 5BZB J0630-2406 belongs to the relatively rare sub-class of high-power flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs). Our results indicate that interactions between protons and external radiation fields can produce a neutrino flux that is within the reach of the IceCube detector. Furthermore, the spectral shape of the X-ray emission suggests the imprint of hadronic processes related to very energetic protons.
